extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy and law (readers of Hobbes' Leviathan)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of Thomas Hobbes' account of what law is, how it is made known and interpreted, the role and required abilities of judges, divisions of law, and the distinctions among sin, crime, and civil obligation. Geared to analyzing or teaching Hobbes' theory of law and sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law is a Command
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law is a Command, and a Command consisteth in declaration, or manifestation of the will of him that commandeth, by voyce, writing, or some other sufficient argument of the same; the Command of the Common-wealth is Law only to those that have means to take notice of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that law derives from the sovereign's will and must be declared; not all persons (e.g., natural fools, children, madmen) are subject to civil law because they cannot understand covenants. The passage links authority to communicative acts (voice, writing, other signs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law Made, If Not Also Made Known, Is No Law
rubrics_metrics.description: A law must be made known to those it obliges; otherwise it is not law to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains obligation only attaches where subjects have means to take notice; gives exemptions (children, madmen, natural fools). Implies a duty on subjects to inform themselves where possible; ties into later sections on registers, proclamations, and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unwritten Laws Are All Of Them Laws Of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: If an unwritten law obliges all subjects without exception and is not published, it is a Law of Nature; likewise, certain unwritten particular instructions known by reason are also natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States natural law is accessible to each person's reason («Do not that to another…»). Uses examples (ministers without written instructions should follow reason; fidelity as part of natural justice). Distinguishes unwritten universal duties from positive law requiring publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must bear manifest signs of Sovereign Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough that a law be written and published; there must be manifest signs that it proceedeth from the will of the Sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against private persons publishing pretend-laws; advises reliance on public registers, public counsels, public ministers, and public seals to verify legislative authority. Emphasises verification of author as part of law's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification versus Authorisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification (testimony and record) is distinct from the Authority of the law, which consists in the Command of the Sovereign only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records/certificates prove that a law exists or was proclaimed; they do not create the law's authoritative force — that is the sovereign's command.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Judge's Sentence Verifies Law in Particular Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When a question of injury depends on the Law of Nature or written law, the sentence of the judge commissioned to hear such causes is a sufficient Verification of the law in that individual case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge's authoritative decision tells parties what the law is for that controversy; distinguishes advice from authoritative adjudication; highlights the judge's role in applying law to facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects ought to consult public registers before acting
rubrics_metrics.description: For questions of injury or crime under written law, every man by recourse to the Registers may be sufficiently informed before he does such injury, or commits the crime; he ought to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposes a duty to inform oneself of written laws when possible; failure to consult when able makes the act unlawful. Also criticises premature complaints made before consulting the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters patent and public seal as verification of officers' authority
rubrics_metrics.description: To obey a public officer it suffices to have seen his Commission with the Public Seale and heard it read, or to have had means to be informed of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies concrete forms (letters patent, public seal) that verify an officer's authority and thereby impose obligations on subjects to behave accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of the law depends on sovereign power
rubrics_metrics.description: The interpretation of all Laws dependeth on the Authority Sovereign; the Interpreters can be none but those which the Sovereign shall appoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that meaning/intent of the law (the 'authentique Interpretation') is located in the sovereign's will; if interpreters are not sovereign-appointed they risk making law contrary to sovereign intent and usurping legislative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: All laws need interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: All Laws, written and unwritten, have need of Interpretation; written laws are obscure because of ambiguous words, and unwritten law of nature needs interpreters due to human partiality and passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why even natural law requires application by impartial reason; stresses the necessity of capable interpreters to apply general principles to particular cases; connects to sovereign's responsibility to resolve knots in law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic interpretation is not that of writers/commentators
rubrics_metrics.description: The Interpretation of the Lawes of Nature in a Commonwealth dependeth not on the books of Moral Philosophy; the Authority of writers, without the Authority of the Commonwealth, maketh not their opinions Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes learned commentary from authorised law; the author's opinions (even if true) are not law unless adopted by sovereign power. Warns against endless commentary proliferating interpretation without sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: The judge giving viva voce sentence in particular cases is the interpreter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Interpretation of the Law of Nature is the Sentence of the Judge constituted by the Sovereign Authority, given viva voce in the act of judicature; that sentence is authentique for the parties pleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies how interpretation operates in practice: judge applies law to the present case; his sentence (given by sovereign authority) becomes law for that dispute, but limited to the parties and instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: A judge's sentence does not bind future judges in like cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Because every judge may err, if in another like case a judge finds the contrary more consonant to equity, he is obliged to do it; no man's error becomes his own law nor obliges him to persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects absolute doctrinal bindingness of precedents: a wrong sentence does not become perpetual law; distinguishes mutable laws vs immutable natural laws; insists judges must study equity anew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between the letter and the sentence (intention) of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between the bare words (letter) and the intendment or meaning (sentence/intention) of the law; the true sense of law is the intentional sense of the legislator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises judges to supply gaps in the letter by reference to the law of nature or legislator's ends when literal words produce incommodity or absurdity; gives examples where literal words must be read in light of intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abilities required in a judge
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities of a good Interpreter/Judge: (1) a right understanding of the principal Law of Nature called Equity; (2) contempt of unnecessary riches and preferments; (3) ability to divest himself of fear, anger, hatred, love, and compassion in judgment; (4) patience to hear, diligent attention in hearing, and memory to retain, digest and apply what he hath heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts judges' required virtues with advocates' skills; notes that many high magistrates need not be learned lawyers but must possess these qualities to judge rightly; includes practical notes about juries and advice from lawyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisions of law (seven sorts, Justinian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven sorts of civil laws: (1) Edicts/Constitutions/Epistles of the Prince; (2) Decrees of the whole people (with Senate); (3) Decrees of the common people (excluding Senate); (4) Senatus consulta (orders of the Senate); (5) Edicts of Praetors and Aediles; (6) Responsa Prudentum (answers/opinions of authorised lawyers); (7) Unwritten customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides analogues to English institutions (proclamations, acts of Parliament, orders of Commons, orders of counsel, chief justices' edicts, reports of cases). Emphasises that divisions are methodological, not natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into Natural and Positive laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural laws are eternal and moral (justice, equity, etc.), while Positive laws are made by the will of those with sovereign power and are either written or made known by other signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that natural law does not require publication and is rooted in reason and morality; positive law is contingent on sovereign will and must be communicated to subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of positive laws: human/divine, distributive/penal
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive laws may be human or divine; human positive laws may be distributive (determine rights) or penal (declare penalties and address ministers/executors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains distributive laws speak to all subjects about property and rights; penal laws address ministers charged with execution of punishment. Discusses divine positive law and problems of how human recipients can be assured of supernatural revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine positive law and its communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine Positive Laws are commandments of God declared to certain people by those whom God hath authorised to declare them; without supernatural revelation particular to a man, assurance of such revelation is impossible except by belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses how subjects may be bound to obey divine laws declared by a human authority: if not contrary to natural law and declared by the commonwealth, subjects may be obliged to obey them as divine law in that political community; uses examples (Abraham, Moses) to show delegation/obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental laws defined
rubrics_metrics.description: A Fundamental Law in every Commonwealth is that, which being taken away, the Commonwealth faileth and is utterly dissolved; laws necessary to uphold sovereign power (war and peace, judicature, election of officers) are fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes fundamental from non-fundamental laws: abrogating fundamental laws destroys the commonwealth, whereas abrogating non-fundamental laws (e.g., subject–subject controversies) does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between Law and Right
rubrics_metrics.description: Lex (law) and Jus (right) differ: Right is Liberty (that liberty which civil law leaves us); Civil Law is an Obligation and takes from us the liberty which the Law of Nature gave us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how civil law limits natural liberty for the sake of protection and social order; frames law as binding obligation contrasted with natural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between a Law and a Charter
rubrics_metrics.description: Charters are donations or grants of the Sovereign and not laws but exemptions from law; the phrase of a law is 'I command', of a charter is 'I have given, I have granted'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that charters confer liberties to particular persons or groups but do not bind the whole commonwealth; distinguishes universal application of law from particular grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Sin
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sin is not only a transgression of a law, but also any contempt of the Legislator; it may consist in commission, omission, speaking forbidden words, or even the intention or purpose to transgress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies scope of 'sin' to include internal purposes (for divine accounting) though Hobbes is cautious about condemning first motions of the mind; distinguishes sin (moral) from what becomes crime subject to human accusation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Crime
rubrics_metrics.description: A Crime is a sin consisting in the committing (by deed or word) of that which the civil law forbiddeth, or the omission of what it hath commanded; every crime is a sin but not every sin a crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that crime requires humanly observable manifestation (deed or word) so that one may be accused; internal intentions unmanifested are sins before God but not crimes in human courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where no civil law is, there is no crime
rubrics_metrics.description: When civil law ceaseth, crimes cease: where there is only natural law, there is no place for accusation — men are their own judges before conscience and can protect themselves by their own power if sovereignty is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives consequences: sin persists under natural law, but civil crime depends on existence of sovereign legal authority; if sovereign power ceases, civil protections and crimes vanish except for those who contributed to that removal (which Hobbes calls a crime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the law of nature excuseth no man
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of every crime is some defect of the understanding, error in reasoning, or force of the passions; ignorance of the law of nature does not excuse a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begins the treatment of excuses and extenuations, indicating subjects are expected to use reason to comply with natural law; sets stage for limits on excuses in matters of moral obligation.
